extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, students of dramatic theory, and scholars of classical drama
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing and analysing classical (Greek-style) tragedy: its fixed structural parts (prologue, episodes, exode, chorus subdivisions), metre/chorus practice, and rules for selecting plot and characters to evoke terror and pity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parts of Quantity of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy hath four Principal Parts, the Prologue, the Epiſode, the Exode, and the Chorus, and the laſt is again divided into Three Parts, which are called Parodos, Staſimon, and Commoi.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These Parts (parts of quantity) have a separate substance, are separately measured, and have fixed places which they cannot change. They denote the different portions that compose the body of a tragedy (contrast with parts of quality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prologue
rubrics_metrics.description: The Prologue is all that part of the Tragedy which precedes the entrance of the Chorus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: to explain to the audience what concerns the subject of the poem and what is proper and necessary; it forms part of the first act. Even where the Chorus enters first, speakers who open the scene may constitute a prologue. The prologue is thus essentially prior to the Chorus's proper singing or duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epiſode (Episode)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Epiſode is that which is between the Songs of the Chorus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically: actors' recitations between chorus songs; evolved into the principal portions of action drawn from the same adventure. In practice the episode contains the progress of the action, intrigues and plot leading toward catastrophe; episodes should be integrated (from the same action) rather than disconnected recitals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exode
rubrics_metrics.description: The Exode is all that which is said after the Chorus has left off Singing, not to begin again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Function: the unravelling and catastrophe of the piece (corresponds to a fifth act). It commonly ends with moral instruction, prayer, or petition; usually short (often only 2–8 verses). It is not typically a place for extended singing; some plays end without chorus discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parodos (first Chorus song / entrance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Parodos is the first diſcourſe of all the Chorus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The parodos (first sung song) normally closes the first act and marks the first interval. The Chorus may speak earlier in the act, but the parodos is the Chorus's first song after being instructed into the action; it should not be confused with preliminary speaking by members of the chorus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staſimon (stasimon)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Staſimon is all that which the Chorus sings after it has taken poſſeſſion of the Stage, and is as it were incorporated in the Action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Musical/metrical note: the stasimon is without anapaests and trochees (slower, more measured metres); it comprises the Chorus's fixed songs within the action (typically the songs after the parodos).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commoi (kommos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Commoi are the Lamentations which the Chorus and the Actors make together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used only in certain tragedies when joint lamentation is natural; named for the gestures (striking oneself) used in such lamentations. They are not present where the subject does not require such tragic lament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity parts are fixed and positional
rubrics_metrics.description: The parts of quantity are separately measured and have a fixed place; they can never be together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is why Greek division (based on Chorus songs and intervals) indicates the different parts composing the body of tragedy more precisely than a mere equal-act division; the placement of prologue, parodos, episodes and exode is structural and meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy's imitation and end (evoking terror and pity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is the imitation of terrible and pitiful things and ought to excite Terror and Compaſſion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The purpose of tragedy is to arouse these passions and thereby refine or purge them; subjects and presentation should be chosen to achieve those effects rather than to produce horror or mere spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character moral status for tragic hero
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragic subject must not make 'a very honest Man fall from Prosperity into Adverſity' nor represent the misfortunes of a very wicked Man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A very virtuous man's fall produces horror (not pity) and undermines the refining effect; a very wicked man's suffering produces neither pity nor fear. The proper tragic subject is a man 'neither bad nor good' (or preferably more good than bad) and of eminent quality or reputation, so that his fortunes can elicit pity and fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose eminent/remarkable persons as subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet ought to choose from those who are of Eminent Quality, and of Great Reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragedy commonly draws subjects from famous families and notable persons (e.g., Oedipus, Thyestes) whose fortunes and fall will carry sufficient weight to move an audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot: single (simple) vs double (twofold) fable
rubrics_metrics.description: A fable which is well composed ought to be simple, and not double; and it ought rather to end with the ill than the good Fortune of the Principal Persons, provided that that Unhappiness be the Consequence of some great Fault and not the Effect of a Remarkable Crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single, unified plot that culminates in a misfortune arising from a significant error (not extreme crime) is proper to tragedy. Double plots leading to paired opposite catastrophes (happy for the good, fatal for the wicked) are nearer to comedy and give a different kind of pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy should be 'complex' (implex) in structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy ought to be Implex and not simple, to have all the Beauty which it is capable of, and that it ought to excite Terror and Compaſſion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'complex' quality here refers to the presence of structural devices (reversals, discoveries, an interconnected causal chain) that intensify emotion — not to having two unrelated plots. Complexity in the sense of well-wrought causal and dramatic turns increases tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus metre and movement correspond to dramatic function
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chorus used different metres: the parodos (first song) employed anapaests and trochees suited to motion; the stasimon avoided these faster metres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meter choice must reflect the movement and function of the chorus: quick metres for motion/entrance, slower measured metres when the chorus is fixed and incorporated into action. The Greeks were precise about matching diction and metre to choreographic/musical movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exode as brief farewell or moral unravelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Some learned men thought the Exode was properly the Epilogue used to thank the company; Aristotle defines Exode as all that is after the last Song of the Chorus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the exode is the concluding unraveling it typically contains moral instruction or prayer; if it were merely a prolonged complimentary farewell it would not constitute a substantive part of the tragedy's quantity.
